svg.aria-label: Diagram: the global external Application Load Balancer in Google Cloud; it is not one proxy but many Google Front Ends, with the same global external address advertised from several points of presence so each client reaches its nearest front end, meaning multiple front ends open connections to your backends and the load balancer address belongs to no single device; every request crosses two separate TCP connections, client to front end and front end to backend, so backends see a Google Front End range rather than the load balancer address, and the traffic between front ends and backends uses special routes not defined in your VPC network; connections are deliberately recycled, with a client keepalive of 610 seconds against a fixed backend keepalive of 600 seconds and long-lived client connections closed at a maximum age of 60 minutes by a connection close header and FIN ACK or an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 GOAWAY frame, without disturbing requests in flight including upgraded WebSockets, while changing the capacity scaler reroutes new requests without closing existing ones; HTTP/2 is chosen by the client when HTTPS is used and cannot be disabled on the load balancer, HTTP/1.0 through HTTP/3 are all accepted, and Google QUIC was removed in April 2023 in favour of HTTP/3 over IETF QUIC; and a port scan of a front end is not an audit, because front ends always show ports 80 and 443 open while refusing connections on ports with no forwarding rule, they answer SYN probes only for configured ports, and one scan interrogates one front end rather than the fleet
svg.title: The global external Application Load Balancer: many front ends behind one address
svg.text: One address, many proxies. “There isn’t just a single proxy.” Almost everything
surprising about this load balancer follows from that sentence.
What “global” actually is: a fleet of Google Front Ends
“In Premium Tier, the SAME global external IP address is advertised from various points of
presence, and client requests are directed to the client’s NEAREST GFE.”
GFEs are “distributed globally, operating together by using Google’s global network and control
plane”, directing traffic to “the CLOSEST HEALTHY BACKEND THAT HAS CAPACITY”.
Consequence: “MULTIPLE GFEs can initiate HTTP(S) connections to your backends”, and “the IP
address of your load balancer isn’t assigned to a single device or system”.
Every request is two TCP connections, not one
1. CLIENT → GFE — destination is your load balancer’s address.
2. GFE → BACKEND — source is a GFE range, destination the backend’s internal address.
So “the source IP address … as seen by the backends, is NOT the Google Cloud external IP
address of the load balancer”. Firewall rules allow GFE ranges, never the LB address.
GFE-to-backend traffic uses “special routes NOT DEFINED IN YOUR VPC NETWORK”.
Connections are recycled on purpose — design for it
KEEPALIVE: client 610s, backend 600s. The client side is CONFIGURABLE; the backend side is
FIXED. The 10-second gap means the GFE, not your server, decides when to let go.
MAX AGE: “a connection is closed when an active client connection reaches a maximum age of
60 MINUTES” — “to ensure that traffic is load balanced evenly”. Not a fault. A policy.
How it closes: Connection: close + FIN ACK on HTTP/1.1, or a GOAWAY frame on HTTP/2 and /3.
“Doesn’t interfere with any active requests or responses, including upgraded WebSocket
connections.” A client that reconnects cleanly never notices.
Changing capacityScaler reroutes NEW requests and closes no existing ones.
The protocol you cannot turn off
“When HTTPS is used, modern clients default to HTTP/2. This is controlled ON THE CLIENT, not on
the HTTPS load balancer. You CANNOT DISABLE HTTP/2 by making a configuration change on the
load balancer.” If HTTP/2 breaks something, fix the client or the backend.
Accepted from clients: HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3. To the backend it is HTTP 1.1,
HTTPS or HTTP/2, per the backend service. 100 Continue is supported.
gQUIC was removed in April 2023; HTTP/3 now rides IETF QUIC.
A port scan of a GFE is not an audit
“GFEs have several open ports to support other Google services that run on the same
architecture.” They ALWAYS show 80 and 443 open, whatever you configured.
But “if you haven’t configured a forwarding rule for port 80 or for port 443, any connections
sent to those ports are REFUSED”. Open in a scan, closed in practice.
“GFEs send SYN-ACK packets … ONLY for ports on which you have configured a forwarding rule”,
and one scan “only interrogates a single GFE per TCP connection”.
“Scanning the IP address of a GFE-based load balancer DOESN’T SCAN ALL THE GFEs in Google’s
fleet.” Regional Envoy-based LBs, by contrast, show no extra ports at all.
Two limits worth knowing before you draw it: a forwarding rule “can reference EXACTLY ONE port
from 1-65535”, so 80 and 443 are two rules. And the CLASSIC variant “only support[s] proxying
over IPv4 to your backends” — dual-stack backends need the global, not the classic, mode.
